title: Parallel dispatch arrays desync on a validation failure, so a request is validated against one route and executed by another
index_line: T-0031 · SQL_EXEC · batch router appends a failure to one array and not the other → handler from a different sub-request runs · php/all-batch-APIs · corroborated
invariant_violated: A batch endpoint assumes that the request it validated is the request it executes, because both are kept in the same loop. But the resolved handler and the validation result live in two parallel arrays: on a validation failure only one of them gets an entry, and every later sub-request is then dispatched with the wrong handler — validation happened against the route the attacker named, execution happened under a route that never saw those parameters.

mechanism.does: an unauthenticated request posts a batch of sub-requests, nesting a second batch inside the first
the dispatcher resolves each sub-request to a route and handler, appending to a matches list, and separately collects validation results
one sub-request fails validation: its error is pushed onto the results list but no handler entry is added, so the two lists no longer share an index

a later sub-request is dispatched using the handler resolved for a different sub-request — nothing enforces the validation-to-handler binding — and that handler maps its parameter into a query variable the *validating* route never declared, so no validation applies to it
a parameter supplied as a string is interpolated into a NOT IN (...) clause, while the array form would have been cast to integers
the query executes and a time- or boolean-based oracle leaks rows the unauthenticated caller could never read

source.http.request.value: the batch envelope plus its sub-requests — the payload is the *shape* of the batch (nested, ordering of the failing sub-request) not a payload string

sink.sql.concat.value: the query variable the displaced handler maps the attacker's parameter into (a NOT IN list is the classic)

guard.none.value: the binding between 'the route whose validator accepted this sub-request' and 'the handler that runs it' — nothing enforces it

encoding.string.value: the type confusion half: the same parameter is safe as an array (cast to ints) and injectable as a string

oracle.timing.value: time-based delay as the extraction channel, because the attacker is unauthenticated and gets no output

preconditions.expr: a batch/multi-call endpoint exists that resolves sub-requests to handlers in a loop
the code keeps the resolved handler and the validation result in separate parallel arrays
a sink-vulnerable handler exists that accepts a parameter the *validating* route does not register — that gap is what the desync buys
platform version is inside the affected range

success: a sub-request naming a route that does not accept the parameter still reaches the handler that uses it
a time-based delay appears only when the batch contains a preceding failing sub-request — that ordering is the proof of the desync
the response for the displaced sub-request is shaped like the other handler's output, not the one that was called
failure_like: the dispatcher rejects the whole batch when any sub-request fails to validate
the handler is resolved and validation results are kept in one record per sub-request — then indices cannot diverge
false_positive: a validation error that merely echoes the parameter — that is the validator working
a delay from a slow endpoint rather than from an injected sleep: calibrate with a baseline request and a non-batch control
an injection that also works without the batch — then it is T-0001 and the desync is not needed

hazards: this is a *dispatcher* bug, not a SQL bug; the same desync gives XSS, SSRF or LFI depending on which handler gets displaced — pick the highest-impact reachable handler
the trigger is an ordering constraint (a failing sub-request must come before the useful one), so probes that send a single clean sub-request will always look negative
type-dependent sanitisation (safe as array, injectable as string) is a second, independent defect — report both halves
batch and multi-call APIs are under-tested because each sub-request looks individually validated
non_transfers: batch implementations that carry one object per sub-request (route, handler, validation) instead of parallel arrays
endpoints where a failed sub-request aborts the batch

evidence.target: WordPress 6.9.0–6.9.4 / 7.0.0–7.0.1 wp2shell chain: CVE-2026-63030 (route confusion) + CVE-2026-60137 (author__not_in SQLi)
